title: How Password Strength Is Estimated: Entropy, Dictionaries, Length
description: How entropy, character sets, dictionaries and length shape password strength scores — and why one formula overestimates, plus where the checker stops.
content:
Password strength is not measured; it is estimated from how many guesses an attacker needs: length and character set define the candidate space, and dictionaries and common-password lists compress that space again. Any score is only the output of a model.

Entropy turns guess counts into bits

Under a uniformity assumption, information entropy is H = log2(N), where N is the number of possible candidate passwords. If a password is assumed to be drawn uniformly at random from a character set of size C for L positions, then N = C^L and entropy is H = L × log2(C). The larger the character set and the longer the password, the larger H; every extra position multiplies the candidate space by C.

This site's tool fixes C at 94 printable ASCII characters (excluding space), which is about 6.55 bits per position. An 8-character password carries about 52 bits of entropy, 12 characters about 79 bits, 16 characters about 105 bits. Switch to lowercase letters only (C=26, about 4.7 bits per position) and the same 8 characters carry only about 38 bits.

Character setBits per position8-character entropy12-character entropy16-character entropy
10 digits3.3226.639.953.2
26 lowercase letters4.7037.656.475.2
62 upper- and lowercase letters plus digits5.9547.671.595.3
94 printable ASCII (excluding space)6.5552.478.7104.9

This table only shows arithmetic: it assumes every character is independent and equally likely. Real passwords rarely satisfy both conditions at once, so it gives an upper bound, not an actual measurement of any particular string.

The character-set assumption decides the score

Password1! is often mistaken for strong: 10 characters, with upper case, lower case, digits and a symbol all present. Against the 94-character set it works out to 10 × 6.55 ≈ 66 bits; but an attacker does not enumerate 94 to the tenth power, they first try the dictionary word password, a capital first letter, and a 1 plus an exclamation mark at the end.

Current NIST and OWASP guidance is: SP 800-63B-4 requires single-factor passwords to be at least 15 characters, at least 8 in multi-factor scenarios, and an acceptable maximum length of at least 64 characters, and it no longer requires forced mixing of upper case, digits and symbols; what it requires instead is comparing candidate passwords against a list of known common and breached passwords. OWASP puts it more directly: long passwords work because they raise the number of guesses an attacker's dictionary or wordlist has to cover, not because of some precise entropy value.

Dictionaries and common passwords pull the whole space back to high-frequency prefixes

A dictionary attack does not enumerate in the order aaaa, aaab; it tries from high probability to low: common passwords, personal names, keyboard paths, years and leetspeak substitutions. This is exactly the set of patterns listed in zxcvbn's design description: spatial sequences such as qwerty and asdf, repeats such as aaaa, sequences such as abcdef and 654321, and case and symbol variations of dictionary words. It models the number of guesses required, and deliberately underestimates.

Breached-password corpora are a second line. Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords lets a client send only the first 5 characters of a SHA-1 hash, the server returns every hash suffix sharing that prefix along with occurrence counts, and the client then compares the full hash locally; this is a k-anonymity query, and the complete password never leaves the local machine. The prefix itself still exposes the candidate range corresponding to a 5-digit hexadecimal value, so what it reduces is the exposure surface of the transfer, not information leakage to zero. To observe this process, you can use the site's Hash Generator to compute the SHA-1 value of a sample and then take the first 5 characters.

The tool's built-in common-password list has only 13 entries:

  • Digits only and repeated digits: 123456, 12345678, 111111, 123123, 000000, 666666, 88888888.
  • Common English words and keyboard paths: password, qwerty, admin, letmein, iloveyou.
  • Short letter-plus-digit combinations: abc123.

Any hit in the list costs 2 points. Real password corpora are far larger than this; the 13-entry list is only a demonstration: a miss proves nothing, while a hit means the password belongs to the small set most often tried.

How much length and character set each contribute

From H = L × log2(C) the difference between the two is directly visible: adding one position multiplies the candidate space by C; adding upper case raises C from 26 to 52, adding digits and symbols raises it to 94, and the gain per position goes from 4.7 bits to 5.7 or 6.55 bits. Taking 8 characters as an example, going from lowercase only to mixed case (C=52) adds only about 8 bits; going from 8 to 12 characters at the 94-character set adds about 26 bits of entropy.

This is also why passphrases get discussed separately: four random words may be twenty-odd characters, and the character set looks like only lowercase letters and spaces, but the candidate space is the size of the wordlist to the fourth power. As long as the words are chosen at random, the length advantage holds; if the words come from lyrics, quotations or personal information, a dictionary attack can cut words out of the phrase just as well. The site's random password generator can produce samples at a given character set and length, for comparison against the table above.

How this site's tool calculates

The tool runs 6 checks: whether the length is at least 8 characters, whether both upper and lower case are present, whether digits are present, whether symbols are present, whether the built-in common-password list is hit, and whether three consecutive characters are present. The score starts at 0: +1 for every 4 characters of length, up to +2; +1 for both cases, +0.5 for digits, +1 for symbols; -2 for a common-password hit, -0.5 for a consecutive-character hit; finally it is rounded and clamped between 0 and 4.

Strength labels have five levels — very weak, weak, medium, strong, very strong — mapping to scores 0 to 4; the strength bar has only four segments and lights them by score. The details panel separately computes an entropy value, estimated fixed as length × log2(94), and gives cracking time in three brackets: above 60 bits it shows “extremely long (over hundreds of years)”, above 40 bits “days to months”, and the rest “seconds to hours”.

CheckWhat the tool decidesWhat it does not cover
Length at least 8 charactersCounts characters onlyDoes not distinguish a random string from repeated characters
Both upper and lower caseAt least one upper-case and one lower-case character (the regex only recognises ASCII [a-z] and [A-Z])Does not judge position or predictability
Contains digitsAny 0–9 appearsDoes not recognise birthdays, years or phone-number fragments
Contains symbolsAny non-alphanumeric character appearsDoes not distinguish common trailing symbols from random ones
Not in the common-password listExact match against 13 entries after lowercasingDoes not cover variations, combinations or larger wordlists
No three consecutive charactersAscending triple, case-insensitiveDoes not cover descending order, skip sequences or keyboard paths

Cracking time is only an order-of-magnitude conversion

Converting entropy into time also means dividing by a guessing rate. The expected number of attempts is about 2^(H−1); at a billion guesses per second, 52 bits is about 2^(51) attempts, that is about 2.25 million seconds, or roughly 26 days; at a trillion per second it is about 37 minutes. For the same string, a thousand-fold difference in the rate assumption means a thousand-fold difference in time.

Online guessing and offline cracking are two different problems. Online guessing is constrained by server-side rate limiting, and NIST lists rate limiting as the main defence against online guessing; offline cracking happens after an attacker has obtained the hash, and its speed depends on the hash algorithm and the hardware — slow hashes such as bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 raise the cost of a single attempt by orders of magnitude. The site's Bcrypt checker lets you adjust the cost rounds and compare the computation delay for the same password at different costs.

The three thresholds are fixed marks that do not move with the rate: the tool puts both 41 bits and 59 bits into “days to months”, yet their actual durations may differ by orders of magnitude. For anything above 60 bits the tool always shows “extremely long (over hundreds of years)”; at about 100 million guesses per second, 60 bits is about 2^59 expected attempts, roughly one hundred and eighty years; at a trillion per second it is about 7 days. The time labels are therefore only good as order-of-magnitude hints.

Why a single formula overestimates

The first assumption of the formula is uniform randomness, the second is independent characters. Real passwords violate both at once: someone picks password and turns it into P@ssw0rd, the characters look complex but the candidate space is concentrated in a few variation rules; append two symbols to 123456 and both length and character set grow, yet a dictionary attack still hits first. zxcvbn's author calls this the way simple strength estimates give bad advice: encouraging only the addition of digits and symbols yields passwords that are only slightly harder for a computer and harder for a person to remember.

This overestimation is visible directly in the tool. correcthorsebatterystaple is 25 characters long, all lowercase, and scores only 2 points (length is capped at 2), showing “medium”; but its entropy is computed against the 94-character set as 164 bits, and the cracking time shows “extremely long (over hundreds of years)”. Conversely, aaaaaaaa is 8 characters, also scores 2 points, has 52 bits of entropy, and shows “days to months”. The first is overestimated by the fixed character-set formula, the second by the length score (its 52 bits is likewise the upper bound of the fixed character-set formula), and each metric covers only its own part of the assumptions.

Boundaries and limits

  • The 13-entry list is only a demonstration. The built-in common passwords are just 13 entries with exact matching after lowercasing; variations, added suffixes and the other million-scale passwords are not in it, so a miss does not mean the password is absent from breach corpora.
  • Entropy is a fixed formula. Whether the actual character set is 10, 26 or 94, the tool computes at 94, so the entropy of a digits-only password is overestimated; for a passphrase the true entropy depends on the wordlist assumption, which the tool does not model.
  • Consecutive characters only recognise ascending triples. 012 to 890, abc to xyz, case-insensitive; descending forms such as 321 and cba, skip sequences such as 135, and keyboard paths such as qwerty do not match.
  • The score is a weighted sum, not a probability. Length is capped at 2 points and each character type adds a fixed amount; after rounding it is clamped to 0–4. It does not compute guess counts, and the dictionary check is only an exact-match table of 13 entries, so the score level only reflects which rules were hit.
  • Cracking time has only three brackets. It is given as the order of magnitude of a full-space offline enumeration at the 94-character set, ignoring hash algorithm, salt, hardware, rate limiting and the attacker's dictionary, and there is no continuous scale between the three brackets.
  • It does not cover attack surfaces beyond the password. Credential stuffing, phishing, password reuse, device-side keyloggers, screenshots, browser extensions reading input, and server-side plaintext storage are not determined by the strength of the password itself, and the tool cannot observe them.
  • Local computation has boundaries. The detection logic makes no network requests and the input is not uploaded to a server; but the page still runs on top of a browser and an operating system, and the input method, clipboard, extensions and screen capture are outside the tool's control. The input field shows characters as dots or asterisks, which is display-layer masking only: MDN explains that type=password replaces each character with a symbol and uses autocomplete to control whether a password manager fills it. Do not paste a real password you are using into any online tool.
  • The result is not a security guarantee. A high score only means fewer rule hits under this rule set, not that the account cannot be compromised; a low score does not mean it will certainly be broken.

Reading the three signals separately

When reading this kind of result, you can separate “entropy upper bound”, “dictionary hits” and “length and character set”: entropy answers how many guesses would be needed if the string were fully random; the dictionary answers whether an attacker can skip most of the space; length and character set answer roughly how large the candidate space is. When the three agree the conclusion is firmer (the dictionary signal here means only those 13 entries), and when they conflict, go with the more conservative one. The value of the tool is that it lays the rules out: what it checks and what it does not check are both visible.

faqs.q: Why does Password1! miss the common-password list yet still count as weak?
faqs.a: Because the common-password check only performs exact matching against 13 entries after lowercasing, while scoring adds points for length and character types, so Password1! gets 4 points. But it is a dictionary word plus a fixed variation, and the attacker's rules try such combinations first; a high score only means many rule hits under this rule set, not that the search space is really large.

faqs.q: Why is the entropy value in the tool fixed to 94 characters?
faqs.a: The implementation has only one formula: length × log2(94), and it does not read the actual character set. Digits-only passwords are therefore overestimated, and for passphrases it depends on the wordlist assumption. It gives an upper bound, not an actual measurement of a particular string.

faqs.q: Why are 321 or cba not judged as consecutive characters?
faqs.a: The built-in regex lists only ascending triples 012–890 and abc–xyz, and is case-insensitive. Descending order, skip sequences such as 135, and keyboard paths such as qwerty are outside the match range, so they do not trigger a deduction.

faqs.q: Does the check send the password to a server?
faqs.a: No. The check performs string tests on the input value inside the browser, and the tool script makes no network requests. But the input method, clipboard, browser extensions and screen capture still run on the local machine and are outside the tool's control, so do not paste a real password you are using into any online tool.
